data.title: FBI's Patel defends change in 'bestiality' hiring practice as lawmakers seek answers
data.description:
FBI's Patel defends change in 'bestiality' hiring practice as lawmakers seek answers

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:31 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, in Washington

1 of 2
FBI Director Kash Patel testifies before a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on oversight of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., September 15, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci

By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - FBI Director Kash Patel told lawmakers on Tuesday he changed the bureau's hiring standards to eliminate bestiality as an automatic disqualifier because he did not want to bar trafficking victims who had been forced to have sex with animals, drawing ‌an incredulous response from Republicans and Democrats alike.

"We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked," Patel said in response ‌to one question during his testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Patel later said that previous regulations disqualified "any individual who participated on either side of it."

"Either side of what, the bestiality?" Senator John ​Kennedy, a Republican, asked. "So you disqualified the animal?"

"We have great canines, but we're not going to disqualify them," Patel said, laughing.

In a more than four-hour oversight hearing, his first appearance before the Senate since May, Patel also faced questions about his agency's handling of files related to the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the use of taxpayer funds for personal travel and allegations that he has politicized the FBI.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But it was his revised hiring standards that drew some of the most noteworthy questions.

"Why would ‌you even get into bestiality?" Kennedy asked, after noting that ⁠prospective FBI agents may be wondering if their political point of view matters. Patel said he was told that some trafficking victims forced into bestiality had been previously disqualified from jobs.

"But you're not telling us today that if a human being had ⁠sex with an animal, they can still be an FBI agent?" Kennedy asked. Patel said no.

Republicans asked Patel about the FBI's probes into a prior federal investigation of Republican President Donald Trump's attempts to overturn his loss to Democrat Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, an issue Republican committee chair Senator Chuck Grassley has called a top priority for the ​panel.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Tuesday's ​appearance came after prosecutor Joe DiGenova, who had been leading a Justice Department investigation that sought ​to show that Trump was the victim of a criminal conspiracy, ‌abruptly resigned last week.

FBI AND ELECTIONS

Patel appeared to confirm media reports that a dozen FBI Iran experts were fired this year because of their alleged "weaponization" efforts, namely that they were part of the investigation into Trump's alleged retention of classified documents.

"I think what's most important is to not have a weaponized FBI," Patel said. "I will endeavor every single day to make sure we have no one there that is doing that."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Patel, a Trump appointee, has been a subject of controversy since he took over as head of the FBI. He drew criticism over media reports about him scuba diving at a Pearl Harbor memorial, and for drinking beer while celebrating ‌with the gold-medal-winning U.S. men's hockey team at the Milan Winter Olympics.

He has also faced scrutiny ​over his use of a government plane and luxury cars, and Trump administration investigations into journalists ​and their sources.

Patel said in a letter released ahead of the hearing ​that he has reimbursed personal travel expenses and said the luxury cars were cheaper than others the FBI has previously bought.

Patel ‌grew increasingly frustrated with Democrats who questioned him over his personal ​conduct, including asking Senator Peter Welch if ​he was hard of hearing.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Everyone sees you for the complete and total fraud you are," Patel told Welch, who was asking whether FBI resources had been used to investigate an Atlantic magazine journalist who had written about Patel's alleged excessive drinking.

Patel also said the FBI would monitor the midterm ​elections from its field offices but told Senator Amy Klobuchar, a ‌Minnesota Democrat, he would follow the law that bars agents from being deployed inside polling places on Election Day.

But Patel later refused to pledge ​that he would not interfere in the election.

"I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies," Patel said.

(Reporting ​by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Will Dunham, Bill Berkrot and Cynthia Osterman)

Marco Margaritoff
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:24 pm UTC

CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten said President Donald Trump has lost a colossal amount of approval from one key voting bloc that helped reelect him in 2024, citing recent polls on Tuesday confirming that prior support from the group has plainly said, "Adios, amigos."

"Oh, my goodness gracious," said Enten during a "News Central" appearance. "Oy oy oy, no bueno if you're the president of the United States, because just take a look here: He had a massive breakthrough in 2024; he won working-class Latinos!"

Politics: Harry Enten Says 1 Key Group Has Sharply Flipped On Donald Trump

Enten cited Pew Research Center data and CNN-SSRS polls from 2026 suggesting Trump, who won the demographic in the 2024 election against former Vice President Kamala Harris, has landed the GOP in major trouble ahead of the upcoming midterms in November.

Advertisement

"He won non-college Latino voters by a point over Kamala Harris," said Enten. "That's a major breakthrough for a Republican president, or a Republican running for president. But that win that he had? Adios, amigos. Goodbye, see you later."

He continued, "Look at his net approval rating now in an average of polls, CNN-SSRS polls across 2026: He's 42 points underwater. That is a switcheroo ... shifting away from the president of the United States, his support rapidly declining, plummeting among working-class Latinos ― a group that helped get him elected back in 2024."

Although Trump won the 2024 election on vows to boost the economy and promises to revive U.S. manufacturing ― and instead launched mass deportations and deadly immigration raids shortly after returning to office — he appears to have lost major support from Latinos since then.

Politics: Harry Enten Spots The 'Bonkers' Way This Group Is Turning On Trump

"There has been a massive, massive backlash," Enten noted Tuesday.

Advertisement

The data guru explained that non-college Latinos helped Trump beat Harris on the issue of immigration by 9 points in the 2024 election, citing an average of CNN-SSRS polls, but now has a net approval rating of -47 points on the issue from that same demographic.

"You don't see shifts away from a president of the United States of 56 points unless you have done something absolutely terribly wrong in the minds of the voters," said Enten. "These are terrible, terrible numbers."

Trump recently hit the worst approval rating of his presidency amid a nationwide affordability crisis that he has repeatedly dismissed and a costly war on Iran that he himself started. Enten noted the resulting backlash from voters should have Republicans "running scared."

"These are the types of numbers that make history for Democrats," he said.

data.title: Texas GOP Sighs, Shrugs As Candidate Fundraises Off Unapologetic Racism
data.description:
Texas GOP Sighs, Shrugs As Candidate Fundraises Off Unapologetic Racism

Ryan Grenoble
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:14 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The race for a relatively obscure statewide office in Texas is gaining national attention after Republican nominee Bo French published a blatantly racist take on the crowd at a University of Texas football game, only to triple down on it amid only tepid pushback from GOP leadership.

French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, kicked off the controversy this weekend by sharing a photo of a group of what appear to be South Asian UT students cheering for the Longhorns on Saturday.

Politics: Trump Administration Potentially Breaking The Law In Non-Citizen Voter Review, Whistleblower Reports

"In the same way HR departments get taken over then exclusively hire in-group, UT seems to be prioritizing the same way," he wrote.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The post went relatively unnoticed, perhaps emboldening French to double, then triple, down and ultimately using it as a fundraiser.

A day later, French shared a different photo of non-white UT students celebrating at the stadium.

"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," he wrote.

Politics: Supreme Court Blocks Trump's Attack On Mail Voting — For Now

In a separate post using the same photo, he later added:

"Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It's everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Texas state law stipulates that 90% of UT Austin's first-year students be state residents. And after a 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision that declared affirmative action unconstitutional, the school is legally prohibited from considering race in its admission process.

Two of the students in the photo told The Dallas Morning News they're U.S. citizens.

"Whether or not we are immigrants, that doesn't change anything," one of them, Rahul Kodali, told the outlet. "I've been an American my entire life."

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

A handful of high-profile Republicans called on French to delete the posts; so far, he's duly ignored them and instead leaned in.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"This is the Republican nominee for statewide office," incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) remarked. "Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad."

Politics: Key Senate Candidate Pounces On Trump's Beef Scheme In New Ad

French responded by saying Cornyn, who lost his primary to Ken Paxton, isn't a true Republican.

Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), a far-right conservative who also lost to a further right candidate in this year's primary, also criticized French's post ― and was similarly ignored.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A handful of state-level Republican lawmakers, including House Speaker Dustin Burrow, called on French to delete the post. No Republicans have called for him to drop out of the race.

State Rep. Drew Darby (R) went further than most, calling French's posts "racism, plain and simple," but stopped short of suggesting he drop out. (His calls for an apology also went unheeded.)

Politics: Court Blocks Texas' Trump-Ordered Gerrymander

Instead, French on Monday leaned on the firestorm as a fundraising prompt.

"!!BREAKING," he wrote in a message directing supporters to his donation page. "The radical left and their allies are attacking me. Join the thousands of patriots who are supporting our campaign here."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It's unclear how well that message is resonating with voters. French's Democratic opponent, oil field engineer Jon Rosenthal, told the Texas Tribune Monday he's seen a surge of donations as a result.

At least one high-profile Republican voter in the state, Karl Rove, said French has lost his vote. Rove, a political consultant and onetime aide to President George W. Bush, reportedly called French a "bigot" at a private lunch event and said he'd be voting for a Democrat for the first time in 30 years.

data.description:
Trump Baselessly Claims Assassination Attempt Was ‘Democrat Plot’ Against Him

Sanjana Karanth
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:14 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

President Donald Trump baselessly claimed on Tuesday that the July 2024 assassination attempt against him was a plot by Democrats, including then-President Joe Biden and FBI Director Chris Wray, to push him out of the election.

The president posted on Truth Social that Biden's FBI "didn't do what they should have with respect to the Lunatic who shot me in Butler, PA," referring to gunman Thomas Crooks, who was 20 years old when he shot at Trump during a campaign rally, grazing his ear, killing a bystander and injuring two others before the Secret Service fatally shot him.

Politics: Donald Trump Says 1 Of His Big Plans For 2026 Is To 'Survive'

"By the time I got into Office, on January 20th, most of the information was missing, altered, corrupted, or gone. New info was just found!" he continued. "This was all a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election, that failed."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump also called Wray, whom he hired to lead the FBI during his first term, a "Dirty Cop" who "should pay a price for the way he handled the assassination attempt, and certainly for the things he said."

Neither Biden nor Wray appear to have responded.

It's unclear what information Trump is allegedly referring to as altered or missing in this startling accusation. Trump suggested months after the shooting that Iran was tied to the attempt, telling rallygoers that if he were president he would tell Iran that "we are going to blow your largest cities and the country itself to smithereens."

Politics: WHCD Shooting Suspect Charged With Attempted Assassination Of President Trump

Biden's FBI swiftly investigated Crooks over the assassination attempt, as well as another apparent attempt that occurred later that year at the Trump International Golf Club in Florida. The former president, as well as many Democrats, denounced the "sick" attempts on Trump's life and condemned all forms of political violence.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The FBI found that Crooks appeared to have acted alone, with no immediate ideological motive, and concluded its probe in November 2025 under Trump's second term.

FBI records provided to Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and reviewed Monday by The New York Post include interviews with Crooks' father, who said his son rarely expressed any emotions and that they "never really had a father/son bond." HuffPost has not independently reviewed the files.

It should be noted that Trump has historically only condemned one side of political violence, having encouraged his followers to storm the Capitol in Washington on Jan. 6, 2021, to prevent Congress from certifying the election for Biden. Trump has pardoned many of the rioters who faced criminal consequences for attempting the insurrection.

data.title: US orbital weapons acknowledgment a landmark moment, US Space Command official says
data.description:
US orbital weapons acknowledgment a landmark moment, US Space Command official says

By Cassell Bryan-Low
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:16 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Space Force Guardians assigned to Space Delta 5 monitor a computer workstation

1 of 3
U.S. Space Force Guardians assigned to Space Delta 5 monitor computer workstations at Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, U.S., December 18, 2025. U.S. Space Forces/David Dozoretz/Handout via REUTERS

By Cassell Bryan-Low

PARIS, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The U.S. Air Force chief's acknowledgment this week that the Pentagon has weapons in orbit is a "landmark" moment in the rising militarization of space aimed at deterring aggression against Washington's allies and economic ‌interests, a U.S. official said.

U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said at a conference near Washington, D.C. on Monday that Washington "has ‌on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," the strongest admission yet by a Pentagon official of U.S. weapons in space amid ​rising space tensions with Russia and China.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The acknowledgment of these space-control capabilities is fundamental to ensuring that we prevent deterrence from failing, and that we are postured and ready should deterrence fail to employ them effectively," Richard Palmer, the director of the Capability and Resource Integration Directorate at U.S. Space Command, said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a space defence conference hosted by consulting firm Novaspace in Paris, Palmer added that there are "some actors across the globe ‌who are very much interested in undermining the ⁠collective interests of the countries and allies gathered here in this audience and across Europe and the rest of the world." He declined to discuss the nature or capability of those weapons.

"The bottom line is that our ⁠joint force and our allied forces require space. Our economies require space," added Palmer. "We are ready in the U.S. to preserve that."

PREPARING FOR WAR IN SPACE

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Air Force secretary's comment underscores how the world's major space powers are preparing for the prospect of conflict extending into space. Satellites have become indispensable ​to ​modern warfare, as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated.

For decades ​they have provided communications, navigation and intelligence services to ‌armed forces on Earth, and once placed in orbit typically remained on fixed paths. Increasingly, however, militaries view them as active weapons platforms capable of launching attacks by disrupting a satellite's operations through jamming or laser dazzling, or even capturing enemy spacecraft.

The head of U.S. Space Command has warned that adversaries are developing capabilities to deny the United States access to key systems and reduce military effectiveness, and that adversaries would likely seek to target U.S. space assets early in a conflict. He has argued that the U.S. must adopt a more active warfighting posture, ‌including calling for orbital interceptors and other weapons.

Some other countries are also looking ​to develop counter-space weapons. That includes Germany, which has a €35-billion ($40-billion) military space spending plan ​aimed at countering growing threats from adversaries.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Major General Michael Traut, ​the head of German Space Command, has previously said that as part of that plan, Germany will channel ‌funding into intelligence‑gathering satellites, sensors and systems designed to disrupt ​adversary spacecraft. Traut said Germany would ​not field destructive weapons in orbit that could generate debris, but said a range of non-kinetic options existed to disrupt hostile satellites, including jamming, lasers and actions against ground control stations.

The U.S. recently conducted a major orbital exercise designed to demonstrate dynamic space ​operations, involving satellites in multiple orbits simultaneously plus ‌participation from international and commercial partners. Called Apollo Maneuvers, it marked the largest such exercise conducted by U.S. Space Command ​both in the number of spacecraft involved and the type of maneuvers performed, a U.S. Space Command spokesperson said.

(Reporting ​by Cassell Bryan-Low in Paris; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Rod Nickel)

data.title: Pennsylvania reports two additional measles-associated deaths
data.description:
Pennsylvania reports two additional measles-associated deaths

By Sriparna Roy
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:13 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Sriparna Roy

Sept 15 (Reuters) - The Pennsylvania Department of Health on Tuesday reported two more measles-associated deaths, both in unvaccinated individuals, bringing the state's total fatalities linked to the disease outbreak to four.

One individual ‌lived in Jefferson County, while the other lived in Mifflin County, the department said, without disclosing any additional ‌details, citing patient privacy. On Sunday, Jefferson County announced that a 40-year-old woman had died of measles complications.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"My thoughts are with the two families who ​lost loved ones to this highly-contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades," said Secretary of Health Dr. Debra Bogen.

Pennsylvania health officials have notified CDC of two additional deaths involving individuals who had measles, a spokesperson for the agency told Reuters, adding that it is in contact with state health officials as they continue to assess these deaths.

Pennsylvania ‌said last month two residents died after contracting ⁠measles, the first such deaths this year in the U.S.

The issue has become politicized as the governor of Pennsylvania and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have publicly argued over the ⁠cases. Kennedy has said only one of the deaths was due to measles.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention does not include the deaths in its measles tally and its website says it is reevaluating how it classifies measles deaths.

Kennedy asked CDC director, Erica ​Schwartz, ​to remove a reference to the two deaths from the agency's ​online measles tally, Reuters reported earlier this month.

U.S. MEASLES ‌CASES SURGE

In 2026, the U.S. has had 3,294 confirmed measles cases through September 10, according to CDC data. Pennsylvania has been the hardest hit with 693 cases in 38 counties.

The Pennsylvania health department said it conducted rigorous investigations with cooperation from the Jefferson and Mifflin County coroner's offices to determine that these cases met the criteria to be considered measles-associated deaths before announcing them.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It reports a "measles-associated death" when an individual with an active case of measles dies and meets a set of ‌criteria.

Those include death within 30 days of symptom onset in an ​individual with clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory ​test, and it is not due to unrelated causes ​such as an accident. Whether an individual was exposed to measles prior to their death or ‌supporting medical records are also considered.

Measles, which can cause ​symptoms including fever, rash and ​respiratory issues, is highly contagious but easily preventable with the measles, mumps and rubella combination vaccine — a routine shot for children that is 97% effective in preventing infection after two doses.

Americans' trust in vaccines for deadly childhood ​diseases, including measles, has fallen in recent ‌years, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

President Donald Trump last month unveiled an executive order that criticized the measles, ​mumps and rubella vaccine, calling for the long-used combination shot to be split up into three separate ​shots.

(Reporting by Sriparna Roy in Bengaluru; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar)

data.title: US Treasury's Bessent says bond yields reflect 'global issues'
data.description:
By David Lawder

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday blamed rising bond yields on "global issues" and confirmed he will meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend ahead of a meeting between President Donald Trump ‌and Chinese President Xi Jinping next week.

Bessent told a hearing of the House Financial Services Committee that Trump and Xi ‌would continue discussions on Iran and China's financial links to Tehran, which Washington has been seeking to shut out of Western financial systems as the war with Iran stretches into ​its seventh month.

The hearing was nominally on the international finance system, including reforms to the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, but lawmakers peppered Bessent with questions about a variety of more pressing issues, like the state of financial markets and the economy, and the administration's punitive financial measures against Iran.

As the hearing got underway, several protesters stood up one after another to call for an end to sanctions on Iran and the war, forcing ‌Bessent to stop and restart his opening statement. ⁠The people were hustled from the room.

Bessent told reporters rising bond yields were due to "global issues," as he headed into the hearing. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yields on Tuesday hit peaks not seen since 2007 amid a ⁠global bond rout experienced by most other large economies.

Analysts tie the U.S. bond yield increase to higher oil prices and expectations the Federal Reserve will raise its policy rate this week, as well as competition for capital from AI spending and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory.

During the hearing Bessent acknowledged the ​rise ​in the 10-year yield reflects "the need to address the deficit," among other things.

U.S. ​bond yields have risen despite recent Treasury buybacks of longer-term ‌debt that Bessent has described as a way to inject liquidity and to counter the rise in yields, or at least slow it down.

Bessent told lawmakers the buybacks were a success and underscored U.S. credibility.

"There is a counterfactual of what would it have done -- and we then proceeded to have the two most successful Treasury auctions that we've had in 20 years," Bessent told the congressional hearing. "Since President Trump has come in, (the U.S. bond market) has been the best-performing bond market in the developed world."

He also defended the Treasury's joint intervention with Japan to shore up ‌its currency, saying the U.S. did it to signal support for Japanese policies.

Several Democratic ​lawmakers pressed Bessent on the state of the economy and rising inflation -- tying it ​to the Iran war and the run-up in global oil ​prices. Bessent blamed inflation on the Biden administration, and insisted Americans are better off under Trump.

He was also asked ‌if Trump's proposal to pay each American $5,000 if Trump's ​Republican party maintains congressional majorities in the ​November election was a serious one. He said he would work with House Speaker Mike Johnson to make those payments happen if congressional approval proved to be needed.

Bessent said the U.S. dollar's strength reflects the Trump administration's credibility.

"A strong dollar is not a ​price on a screen; it is a set ‌of behaviors, and what we have seen in this administration, where we are creating regulatory certainty, tax certainty, trade certainty ​and energy certainty that is bringing in trillions of dollars into the U.S.," Bessent said.

(Reporting by David Lawder; Writing by ​Susan Heavey and Ann Saphir; Editing by Doina Chiacu and Andrea Ricci)

data.title: Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month, CBO says
data.description:
Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month, CBO says

By Jacob Bogage
Tue, 15 September 2026 at 6:01 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Jacob Bogage

WASHINGTON, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The six-month-old U.S. war against Iran has cost $38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by $3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ‌ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.

The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in ‌the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totaled expenses through August 1.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The mounting costs have strained U.S. munitions stockpiles and driven up energy ​prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.

The cost was close to the $37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on July 21.

The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish U.S. stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the U.S. had ‌used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the ⁠war.

The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.

The inquiry was conducted at the request of the ⁠top Democrat on the U.S. House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.

"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American ​taxpayers ​tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."

Eighteen ​U.S. military service members have died in the Iran war.

The ‌report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on U.S. military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.

IMPACT ON US READINESS

The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the U.S. defense posture and the domestic economy.

The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving ‌China and Taiwan, CBO said.

"Without these funds, we face critical ​shortfalls," Hegseth said.

Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of ​Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war — and on ‌energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices ​for consumers and global producers.

The rising ​cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating U.S. fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed $40 trillion in August.
